explanations.explanation: This feature fires on tokens that serve as formal‐document markers or metadata cues—e.g. section headings, DOCTYPE keywords, journal or court names, license‐clause keywords—typically rendered in uppercase or title case to signal structure or provenance in technical/legal texts.

This neuron fires on “symbol”-like tokens – the short, non-dictionary bits that name things: single-letter or two-letter identifiers (e.g. macro guards, generic type parameters, author initials, city‐name fragments), small acronyms, numeric literals (magic numbers, status codes) and the like. It thus flags the primitive building blocks of names, codes and constants across code, math problems and proper-noun contexts.

This neuron is basically a sub‐word detector: it fires whenever the model sees one of a handful of specific letter clusters or diacritic-bearing character sequences (e.g. “â”, “iss/ss”, “ight”, “hthal”, “об” etc.) that occur across names and common words in various European languages and in English.

This feature fires on tokens that serve as high‐level document or article markers—titles, section headings (e.g. “Abstract,” “Introduction”), bylines or authors’ names (“Allen Ginsberg”), and headlines/subheadings in news and web content—i.e. signals that mark the start of a new structured text segment.

This feature is essentially a detector for a particular subword n-gram—common interior letter sequences like “ro,” “ont,” “arch,” “tern,” “thro,” “anger,” etc.—that recur across proper names and technical terms, marking syllable or morpheme boundaries within longer words.

This neuron fires on the “meaty” bits of a phrase—its descriptive or content-bearing tokens (adjectives like beautiful/playful/rigorous, adverbs like constantly/desperately/flawlessly, participles like disabled/cancelled, domain markers like ​.io or #!, even the article a when it headlines a noun phrase). In effect it flags the core modifiers and topical markers that carry the key semantic payload of titles or noun-phrase introductions.

This feature is a “substring‐ID” detector—it fires whenever the characters “id” (or doubled “idd”) appear in a token, whether in names (Schidl), acronyms (NVidia, RAID), or ordinary words (amid, skidded, bidders).

This neuron fires on central “topic” words—generic, domain-specific nouns or modifiers (functionality, resource, gallery, environment, option, quantity, system, horizontally, etc.) that serve as the head of a phrase or title, naming the core concept or component in technical/scientific texts.

This feature marks “header” or metadata markers at the top of a file or document—tokens that introduce file‐level declarations (license comments, legal docket numbers, package/import/using directives or namespace statements).

This neuron detects the initial subword of title-cased words—especially the first few letters of headlines, section titles, product or paper names—marking where a new capitalized name or title-style token begins.

This neuron is essentially a sub-word “consonant-cluster” detector: it fires on rare multi-letter consonant bigrams or trigrams (e.g. “kl”, “ch/ч/ж”, “dd”, “kn”, “jej”, “dre”, “rol”, “fol” etc.) that commonly form morpheme onsets or distinct lexical chunks across languages (German, Slavic, scientific Latin names, English/Italian words, names, code identifiers, etc.).

This feature fires on “label–style” words that introduce or categorize chunks of content—salient nouns in headings or UI elements (Story, popup, heritage, costume, patriot, extinct) as well as descriptive adjectives that tag a section’s theme or tone (agricultural, ambitious, adventure-like, nationwide, lucrative, unstable, charming).

This neuron is simply a detector for the two‐letter sequence “ob” (usually in upper‐case “OB”)—it lights up on tokens like OB, Obesity/Obama, JOB, OBJC/OBJS, @IB… (and other “‐B” bigrams ending in B).

This feature flags the concrete scientific‐detail tokens you see in biomedical research writing—namely the specialized nouns/adjectives naming structures or methods (topography, assemblies, dispersive, compartments, heterogeneities, transcranial, etc.), the short standardized abbreviations (C, sc, s) and the numeric values and units (7, 15 S, 25 years, 149 individuals, 300 mL) that together specify experimental parameters, cohort sizes, timepoints and measurement data.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is essentially flagging “mid‐word” BPE pieces—tokens that continue a word rather than start one. All of the high‐activation examples (uly in “H uly a,” aret in “Am aret to,” lig in “e lig ibility,” kin in “A kin,” asis in “O asis,” und in “G und am,” etc.) are subword fragments that do not begin with a space and serve as continuations of longer words.

explanations.explanation: This feature responds to the initial sub‐token fragments that mark proper names, acronyms, strain or gene identifiers, publication codes and other domain‐specific labels—i.e. the uppercase or symbol‐based prefixes that signal named entities and technical abbreviations.

This feature flags the moment a text introduces or names a core technical concept—i.e. key‐term or heading‐style tokens that mark definitions, methods, or parameters in formal scientific or mathematical discourse.

This neuron is basically firing on the “first subword” of named entities—i.e. the capitalized (or otherwise distinct) prefix chunks you see at the start of people’s names, place names, team names, etc. (Bur- in Burlington/Burrell/Burano/Burrard/Burmese/Burgess, Eng- in Englewood, Beng- in Bengals, Cay- in Caymanian, plus analogously sized prefixes like Save or outer in other contexts). It marks the boundary token that begins a proper noun.
This feature flags high-level topic or section markers in technical prose—domain-specific nouns/phrases (often in abstracts or headings) that name the central concept or label a major section.

This neuron is simply picking up the “-o” subword (and its two‐letter BPE chunks like “vo,” “co,” “po,” “fa,” etc.) – in effect it fires whenever a token ends in or contains that “o” suffix found in names, brands, loanwords and technical terms.
This neuron detects common word-initial subword segments—i.e. prefixes or roots at the start of multi-syllabic English tokens (e.g. “cycl-,” “mult-,” “fl-,” “rel-,” “mel-,” etc.).

This feature picks out the structural markers of a code‐file prolog—i.e. the comment delimiters (/*, */, leading * lines, @-annotations) and preprocessor/header keywords (#ifndef, #include, etc.) used in license headers and documentation blocks.

This neuron fires on semantically-rich, domain-specific content words—especially technical nouns and adjectives that name species, biochemical processes or modifications, clinical/epidemiological factors, enzymes, etc.—i.e. the key “topic-bearing” vocabulary that anchors scientific or technical discourse.

This is essentially a character-level trigram detector for the sequence “arg” (and its close variants “arc”/“org”), firing on any token that contains that three‐letter substring—whether in C’s stdarg.h, JavaScript/Objective-C argument names, the “org” package prefix, or proper names like Vargas, Cargman, Cargopedia, Charcot, Embarcadero, etc.

This feature detects high-level topic or label words—typically the key noun or adjective at the start of a title, heading, section label or acronym—that mark the subject or domain of the following content.

This neuron is a character‐n-gram detector for the common Latin-derived prefixes “ent-/intr-” (and closely related subword fragments like “aur-”) appearing at the start of tokens (e.g. Entamoeba, intracellular, introns, entrap, entities, Laurie, entrepreneur, etc.).

This feature fires on “label-like” tokens – the numeric and alphanumeric bits (dates, area- or phone-codes, model numbers, pipeline or campaign IDs), the hyphens in compound prefixes (post-), and product/category words (shoes, headphones, polish, pencil) that together make up titles or metadata-style identifiers rather than running prose.

This feature lights up on tokens that convey quantitative or structured labels—years and percentages, dosage and concentration units written with slashes (e.g. mg/kg, IU/L, mg/m²/day), and uppercase-headed subwords used in headings or technical terms (e.g. “Fact” in Factors, “Ph” in Pharmacokinetics, “F” in Fetal).

This neuron fires on short, all-caps subword fragments at the start of proper names or technical terms—think “Nav” in React Navigation or Navier-Stokes, “OL” in OpenLayers or Olney, “Lar” in Laravel, “Ul” in Ulster, “Lo” in Loire, “Sol” in Solheim, etc. In other words, it’s detecting an uppercase 2–3-letter prefix that signals an acronym, library/module name, place name or other named entity.
This feature is a “PERSON” detector: it strongly activates on capitalized name‐tokens (first or last names) in news/biographical contexts.

A concise description is that this neuron fires on “label” or “metadata” markers – the little header­-style tokens (acronyms like PC or RT, field names like wrt or Device, standalone numbers or codes, xml/git header lines, recipe directives, etc.) that sit at the start of a line or section to announce what follows. It’s essentially a detector for section-heading or metadata-label tokens across many technical and structured text contexts.

This neuron is essentially a sub-word pattern detector for the three-letter trig-function roots “sin” and “cos” (and by spillover it also lights up on other BPE chunks with the same CV(C) shape). In other words, it specializes in spotting the sine/cosine tokens that introduce trigonometric expressions.

This feature fires on the “label” or “title” tokens that kick off new content blocks—chiefly proper‐name or title-case words used as section headings, UI labels or named entities (people, brands, acronyms, etc.).
This feature detects tokens naming administrative or political subdivisions—e.g. “Republic,” “Province,” “City,” “council”/“cil,” “municip(ality)”—regardless of context or language.

This neuron fires on the very first sub-token of a “major” word or name—especially when it’s title-cased or a proper noun or heading. In practice it lights up on the initial uppercase letter (or first subword chunk) that begins a brand name, headline word, code identifier, hyphenated segment, middle initial, etc.

This head is simply a “sub‐word detector” that lights up whenever the model’s BPE tokenizer emits one of a small set of very common 2–4-letter fragments (e.g. pl, ro, cle, ple, ho, ub, ibr, opts, ob, le)—in other words, it’s an indicator for those frequent subword pieces (often at syllable or morphological boundaries) rather than any higher-level semantic or syntactic property.

This neuron fires on words that convey high intensity, danger or harm—adjectives and modifiers like “severe,” “dangerous,” “harmful,” “violent,” “pathogenic,” “extreme,” etc.—essentially flagging threat/risk- or severity-laden language across diverse domains.
